coach.board: Each tile is a pod, grouped by the node it runs on. The strip shows how many requests succeed each tick.
coach.actions: The buttons scale, roll back or edit the web deployment, and the prompt runs kubectl. Reading is free; changing the cluster costs a move.
coach.firstMove: Run kubectl get pods, click any pod that is not Running to describe it, then fix what it tells you.

events.title: The chaos monkey killed a pod
events.fix: The Deployment's ReplicaSet notices the missing pod and starts a replacement on its own. With a readiness probe and a spare replica nothing is lost, so acting here only wastes time.

events.title: A bare Pod was killed and nothing brought it back
events.fix: A Pod created directly isn't self-healing; only a controller recreates pods. Put the workload under a Deployment (here: scale the Deployment up to replace the lost capacity).

events.title: A rollout pointed the Deployment at an image tag that doesn't exist
events.fix: The new pods can't pull the image, so the rollout stalls and the old pods it already retired aren't replaced. kubectl rollout undo returns to the last working revision.

events.title: A rollout changed the pod label to the wrong value
events.fix: The pods run fine but no longer match the Service's selector, so the Service has no endpoints for them. Fix the label to match the selector (or roll back).

events.title: A rollout referenced a ConfigMap key that doesn't exist
events.fix: The container can't even be created (CreateContainerConfigError), so there are no logs to read: kubectl describe pod and its Events name the missing key. Correct the key (or roll back).

learn.section: Consuming them: env vars vs. volume mounts

events.title: A release needs more memory than the pod's limit allows
events.fix: Going over a memory limit gets the container OOMKilled (CPU would only be throttled). The new pods crash-loop while the old ones keep serving: raise limits.memory above what the app needs, keeping requests at or below limits.

events.title: A release shipped without a readiness probe
events.fix: With no readiness probe a pod counts as ready the moment its container starts, so the Service sends traffic to pods that are still warming up. Add the probe (or roll back).

events.title: A batch job grabbed the nodes' memory and a web pod was evicted
events.fix: The scheduler places pods by memory requests, and none is left, so the replacement stays Pending. Free capacity by scaling the noisy batch Deployment down, or lower the web pods' requests.

events.title: A hardening change set runAsNonRoot on an image that runs as root
events.fix: The kubelet refuses to start a container that would run as root when runAsNonRoot is true. Prefer an image built for non-root (web:1.0-nonroot) over weakening the setting, or roll back.

levels.title: 1. Tutorial
levels.blurb: One problem at a time, with hints. Look first (kubectl get pods, kubectl describe), then act. Keep the Service healthy for 30 ticks.
hints: Look at the pod tiles: a pod that is not Running is your lead. Click one to describe it.
A bad rollout leaves the new pods failing while the old ones are fine, and a pod restarts because of a missing setting.
Run kubectl rollout undo deploy/web, then use Edit to add the missing environment key (mode).

schedule.hint: A pod died. Run kubectl get pods and watch what the Deployment does before touching anything.
The rollout is stuck. kubectl get pods shows why; kubectl describe pod <name> shows the Events.
Pods fail to start. kubectl describe pod <name> and read the Events at the bottom.

levels.title: 2. Shift
levels.blurb: No hints and overlapping trouble. One of your pods is a bare Pod (legacy-web) and the release process is sloppy. Survive 45 ticks.
hints: Look at the pods and the node bars: restarts and Pending pods point at memory and at rollouts.
legacy-web is a bare pod, so nothing replaces it; the memory limit is too tight, and a release is bad.
Scale web to 3, roll back the bad release, raise the memory limit with set resources, and add a readiness probe in Edit.

levels.title: 3. Incident night
levels.blurb: Compound failures: a noisy neighbour, a bad rollout and a security change land close together. Survive 50 ticks.
hints: Look at the node bars first: a noisy neighbour is eating the memory the web pods need.
Three things overlap: the batch deployment crowds out web, a web rollout is bad, and a security change now needs a non-root image.
Scale batch to 0, undo the web rollout, switch the image to web:1.0-nonroot in Edit, and raise the memory limit.
